title: The (Mis)behaviors that Undermine Our Credibility
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that teacher credibility is the wildcard of student motivation, because students only take seriously a teacher's messages about effort, value and success if they believe the teacher. He leans on Hattie's meta-analysis for credibility's impact and then borrows a study by Banfield, Richmond and McCroskey that sorts credibility-killing teacher misbehaviors into incompetence, indolence and offensiveness. The lists are concrete, running from mispronouncing names and overloading students to playing favorites and using sarcasm, and the study ranks offensive behaviors as most damaging. Stuart adds classroom mismanagement to the incompetence list from his own experience. He frames credibility as the lazy teacher's route to motivation, since earning it makes every later motivational move work better. The post ends by asking teachers, and non-classroom educators with their own colleagues, to audit which listed behaviors they commit.
points: Credibility is presented as the multiplier on every other motivational effort, so protecting it pays off more than any single motivational trick.
The research sorts credibility-killers into incompetence, indolence and offensiveness, with offensive behaviors such as humiliation, favoritism and sarcasm doing the most damage.
Late papers and missed test dates hurt credibility least, which suggests students forgive sloppiness more readily than disrespect.
Stuart's 'lazy teacher' framing treats credibility as an efficient investment because it makes every later message from the teacher land.
The same audit works for coaches and administrators, who can ask which of these misbehaviors erode their credibility with teachers.
quotes: The wildcard of student motivation, in any given classroom, is teacher credibility. If kids believe you, they’re going to earnestly consider what you have to say, whether it’s about the content they’re learning or the other four key beliefs.

As hokey as it sounds, teacher credibility’s impact on student achievement is well-established in what is probably the least hokey of all educational studies ever conducted: John Hattie’s Visible Learning meta-analysis. (I discuss that a bit more here.) Credibility is the secret sauce of impactful classrooms.

Here are some ways to undermine your credibility, according to an interesting study from Sara Banfield, Virginia Richmond, and James McCroskey. (There’s a pdf of the study here.) The authors group credibility-killing “misbehaviors” into three categories: incompetence, indolence, and offensiveness.

The study found that indolent misbehaviors are the third most-effective way to undermine your credibility. In other words, these have the smallest negative impact on credibility, perhaps because these behaviors tend to make a teacher’s course easier.

My grandpa always said that he was successful because he was lazy. It sounds bad, but what he meant is that he wasn’t ever content to simply achieve a goal — he wanted to achieve it as simply as possible.

This is why I bring Grandpa’s laziness up: teacher credibility is the lazy teacher’s approach to student motivation. If you can become credible in the eyes of your students, you can expect that telling them to believe the other key beliefs of motivation will actually do something.

And for my folks outside of the classroom, consider job-appropriate, correlative misbehaviors to the list above. The teachers you work with are motivated by the same five key beliefs — how might your (mis)behaviors be unintentionally undermining your credibility with teachers?
